articles.title: Under the Gun: Understanding America’s Defense Spending Paradox
articles.body:
On May 9, 1915, more than 11,000 British troops were killed or wounded in a single day during an ill-fated assault on an entrenched German position in Aubers, France. The reason for the disaster: a shortage of artillery shells to support the assault, particularly the high-explosive shells best suited for trench warfare. The resulting “Shell Crisis of 1915,” led to a major reorganization of the British government’s defense production system. It still wasn’t enough to prevent the fall of Prime Minister H.H. Asquith a year later.
The shell crisis of World War I reminds us just how hard it is to prepare for long wars. “In almost every war there comes a point when it's clear that the peacetime defense industry, even if it had been ramping up, is inadequate for the demands of war,” says Mark Cancian, a retired Marine Colonel who is now a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
More than a century later, the world, and warfare, have changed. But even in a world of fighter jets, nuclear weapons, satellite communications, drones, and AI, ammunition still matters. The decline of the British Empire was followed by the rise of the United States as Earth’s military superpower, the Cold War's onset and end, and numerous conflicts throughout the Middle East. Now, America faces an arms shortage of its own. Even given the historical precedent, the current U.S. predicament is stunning.
The United States spends more on defense than the next seven countries combined, including rivals China and Russia. And yet, the U.S. military finds itself concerned about running short of key munitions in a war with a country, Iran, that could generously be described as a “middle” power.
In August, Reuters reported that the United States had used up “virtually all” of its long-range precision weapons during five months of fighting with Iran. The U.S. also reportedly used more than two-thirds of its supplies of Patriot interceptors in the Middle East, and the global Patriot shortage has in turn left Ukrainian cities dangerously vulnerable to Russian strikes.
President Donald Trump has angrily insisted that the U.S. has “virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition.” However, the Pentagon’s own accounting tells a different story. An inspector general’s report in September admitted that the war had revealed “strategic inventory shortfalls.” Warnings from his senior military commanders about the state of U.S. stockpiles were reportedly one major reason why Trump has refrained from a return to full-scale combat against Iran.
If that’s what a few months of combat with Iran does to U.S. stockpiles, it’s hard to be optimistic about a potential war with China. A CSIS report warns that the U.S. would likely run out of some types of long-range missiles after just a week of combat in a war over Taiwan.
All of this begs the question: How is it possible that the most expensive military in the history of the world doesn’t have enough ammunition to fight a war?
American ammunitions
The origin of the current munitions miseries is often traced back to a particular night in 1993, when Deputy Secretary of Defense William Perry invited defense industry executives to a secret dinner at the Pentagon, which came to be known as the “Last Supper.” Perry warned the executives that Cold War-era defense budgets were no longer sustainable and predicted that many of them would likely go out of business.
Perry’s prediction proved correct. Between 1988 and 1997, defense budgets fell by around 30% and about a dozen major U.S. defense contractors consolidated into four. Much of those budget cuts were taken out of funding for new weapons as the military drew down on Cold War-era stocks.
But the issue wasn’t just money. In the decade following the 9/11 attacks, U.S. defense spending more than doubled, though even amid growing tensions with China and Russia, it’s still less than half of 1980s budgets. But even with budgets creeping up toward a trillion dollars, dividing up the pie is harder than you’d think. Operations costs, maintenance, and spending on military personnel—including pay and retirement benefits—consume a significant portion of the U.S. defense budget. When it comes to what’s left, new high-budget platforms—aircraft, ships, planes—were often prioritized over munitions supplies.
“For many years, in internal defense budget deliberations, to find savings to meet the overall target, munitions were often the ‘bill payer,’” says William LaPlante, who served as Under Secretary of Defense for acquisition and sustainment in the Biden Administration.
The decisions were made easier by the fact that the wars being fought against insurgent groups in Iraq and Afghanistan didn’t require the same amount of missiles, shells, and air defense interceptors needed for a war against a nation-state military.
All that changed with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, sparking a war featuring the kind of artillery use not seen in Europe since the days of the Battle of Aubers, as well as missile barrages on Ukrainian cities requiring a massive number of interceptors. All of a sudden, munitions were in high demand. After years of declines in America’s defense industrial base and manufacturing capabilities, increasing production of artillery shells as well as more advanced missiles and interceptors has been a frustratingly slow process.
What happened to the economic principle that supply rises to meet high demand? Defense companies have been reluctant to build out production capacity for new wars when the demand may disappear in a year or two. Indeed, it may even behoove some defense companies to stick to a high-demand, low-supply, high-margin business model. The impact for Americans, though, is that the cost to taxpayers stays high, even as the military struggles to keep up with the resource demands of modern combat.
Blaming and buzzwords
Trump, for his part, has blamed Biden’s decision to supply Ukraine for the current shortages in the war with Iran. This is misleading: the vast majority of the weapons systems sent to supply Ukraine’s land war are of little use in the war in Iran. A notable exception is advanced air interceptors like Patriots, which are at a premium in both conflicts.
Both conflicts have made clear that the economics of using multimillion-dollar interceptors to knock down cheap cruise missiles and drones—akin to “throwing Ferraris at frisbees,” as Rep. Ted Lieu memorably put it—are brutally expensive for the defending side.
These days, the buzzwords for defense planners, as well as the crop of Silicon Valley-linked defense startups that have emerged in this post-Last Supper era, are systems that are “attritable,” meaning cheap and replaceable, and “modular,” meaning they can be easily adapted for future wars. Plans for the defense of Taiwan, for instance, involve building swarms of cheap and most likely AI-controlled drones to create a “hellscape” for Chinese invaders. But given how fast battlefield technology and tactics are advancing, even those plans may soon be obsolete. 
“The whole system has to be shaken up because the move, counter-move cycle in modern warfare is eye-wateringly short, and we are not prepared,” says Mackenzie Eaglen, a defense analyst and senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. 
In response, the Pentagon has announced a series of steps to speed up weapons acquisition by centralizing buying authority and cutting red tape. Though some of the plans have received pushback from Congress over the new powers being claimed by the department and concerns that it will incentivize companies to deliver inferior products quickly, it’s notable that virtually nobody is standing up to defend the old system—and changing this system will likely be a significant challenge in its own right.
Too few shells, or too many wars?
Analysts often use the phrase “turning an aircraft carrier” to describe the challenge of reforming the bureaucratic behemoth that is the Pentagon and defense industry for a new age of warfare. The metaphor became literal earlier this year when the USS Ford was diverted from the Mediterranean to Venezuela and then back to the Middle East again as the administration jumped from one conflict to another. The ship would spend a record 326 days at sea—a mission that included food shortages, sewage leaks, and a nearly disastrous fire.
The logistical challenges of deploying the US Navy’s limited number of aircraft carriers, as well as concerns about munitions stockpiles, are reminders that even the world’s most powerful military is constrained by scarce resources, particularly given the growing number of wars it has been fighting lately.
The Pentagon has prioritized the production of 14 critical munitions in its spending priorities, but it’s still going to have to compete with big-ticket priorities, including Trump’s dreams for a $1.2 trillion “golden dome” missile defense system, a new focus on space-based weapons, and nuclear modernization. Even with a proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget, it’s going to be difficult to do all those things while fighting one, if not more, ongoing military conflict—as well as preparing for a potentially much larger one to come.
What if the problem is less how the U.S. prepares for wars than the wars themselves? “Restrainers” on both the left and right argue that the munitions crisis should prompt a rethinking of whether the U.S. should get involved in as many armed conflicts as it does and whether it can credibly commit to defending allies in a potential superpower conflict with China.
Money can buy you a lot of firepower, but it doesn’t exempt you from the need to make real choices about priorities.

articles.title: Allies Press Greece, Spain for Expiring Patriot Missiles
articles.body:
NATO and EU officials are lobbying Greece and Spain to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles nearing the end of their operational shelf life to Ukraine, The Telegraph reported.
Athens and Madrid hold some of Europe’s largest national inventories of Patriot PAC-2 interceptors, weapons that Ukrainian defense planners urgently require to protect urban population centers and energy infrastructure from Russian ballistic and cruise missile strikes.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
President Volodymyr Zelensky previously stated that Ukrainian forces require between 300 and 360 Patriot interceptors to withstand anticipated winter bombardments.
According to military records cited by The Telegraph, Greece holds at least 200 Patriot PAC-2 missiles whose certified 23-year operational lifespan is approaching expiration. While the exact quantity held in Spanish military depots remains classified, Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares confirmed last month that Madrid would deliver five interceptors to Kyiv.
Allied defense coordinators argue that transferring aging munitions before they surpass statutory shelf limits represents a pragmatic solution for both donor nations and Ukraine.
Patriot interceptors carry manufacturer-guaranteed shelf lives during which performance is certified; once that operational window elapses, the missiles must undergo expensive and logistically intensive factory recertifications.
Medvedev Warns Against Travel to Europe, Claims It Is ‘Targeting Russians’
“We know that some countries have interceptor missiles that will expire soon,” EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas said during multilateral consultations in Ireland last month. “So it would be very good if they were transferred to Ukraine.”
Global Patriot shortfalls and US-Iran conflict
The diplomatic initiative to unlock southern European stockpiles arrives as Western defense planners confront severe bottlenecks in interceptor manufacturing, compounded by ongoing military operations involving the United States in the Middle East.
Ukraine historically relies on a NATO-coordinated framework for roughly 95 percent of its Patriot interceptors, a mechanism under which European partner governments pool financial resources to purchase replacement missiles directly from American production lines.
However, heavy expenditure of surface-to-air missiles during the US conflict with Iran has precipitated a severe global inventory deficit.
US military stockpiles of Patriot missiles have fallen to fewer than 1,700 units, fueling doubts among European allies regarding the Pentagon’s willingness to release additional interceptors from strategic reserves while active combat operations in the Middle East continue.
With US supply lines backlogged by multi-year production lead times, Western defense coordinators have intensified efforts to identify existing surface-to-air missiles stored within European arsenals that can be deployed to Ukrainian batteries immediately without degrading the conventional defense readiness of donor nations.
Eastern flank reinforcement
The scramble to source interceptors for Ukraine coincides with expanding NATO deployments to protect the primary logistical conduits funneling Western military assistance across the Ukrainian border.
On Tuesday, Oct. 6, the Swedish government announced that Sweden will deploy a Patriot air defense battery alongside approximately 100 military personnel to southeastern Poland in December.
The Swedish detachment, drawn from the Air Defence Regiment with support from the Blekinge Air Wing, will be stationed around Rzeszów, the principal transit hub through which international military aid and humanitarian cargo enter Ukraine.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson confirmed that the system – designated domestically as Air Defence System 103 – will operate under NATO Air Command as part of the alliance’s Integrated Air and Missile Defense network through the end of 2026, with planning underway to extend the mission into 2027.
The ground battery supplements Swedish JAS 39 Gripen multirole fighters that integrated into NATO air policing over Poland earlier in October.
The allied mission in Rzeszów aligns with broader moves by Warsaw to reinforce Poland’s eastern boundary, including the positioning of Polish Patriot units in the Lublin region to deter airspace incursions as Russian standoff strikes continue along the Ukrainian frontier.

articles.title: Report: Iran rebuilds missile and drone factories, replenishes arsenal despite US-Israeli strikes
articles.body:
Iran has managed to preserve its missile and drone production facilities despite months of U.S. and Israeli airstrikes, allowing it to replenish its weapons stockpiles, Bloomberg reported Saturday, citing officials familiar with Western intelligence assessments. Western officials who spoke on condition of anonymity said Tehran retains the ability to manufacture weapons and rebuild its arsenal.
One official said Iran remains "well-stocked" with ballistic missiles and certain anti-ship weapons and can rapidly produce additional missiles. The official also said Russia has been supplying missiles to Iran, consistent with intelligence assessments reported in June. Russia's Defense Ministry did not respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.
The findings suggest that Iran has retained significant weapons production capabilities even as U.S. President Donald Trump refrains from launching further strikes ahead of November's midterm elections. The assessment contradicts repeated claims by Trump and senior administration officials that eight months of airstrikes have destroyed Iran's ability to threaten American military bases in the region and U.S. allies.
Earlier this year, Trump declared that Iran's military had been "totally destroyed." In a September 30 speech, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the United States had destroyed Iran's "military industrial capacity" and "their entire defense base." The latest findings raise the prospect that Tehran could further rebuild its missile forces if Trump follows through on his pledge, announced on social media Thursday, not to attack Iran before the November elections.
Meanwhile, Iran has intensified attacks on commercial shipping around the Strait of Hormuz. According to the British Navy, at least 10 vessels have been struck over the past week. Responding to Bloomberg's report, a White House spokeswoman rejected its findings.
"President Trump completely obliterated Iran's nuclear facilities during Operation Midnight Hammer," she said. "Then, during Operation Epic Fury, he successfully destroyed the conventional shield Iran sought to build around its nuclear program, including its ballistic missiles, production facilities and navy."
The report comes as Washington continues to weigh renewed military action against Iran despite Trump's public commitment to avoid further strikes before the elections. The New York Times reported Thursday that the U.S. military was preparing for the possibility of another large-scale offensive against Iran, with Pentagon planners developing options for an intensive military operation lasting approximately three days.
Despite extensive preparations and escalating Iranian attacks on oil tankers, Trump has remained reluctant to resume large-scale hostilities. In recent months, he has rejected five separate proposals for major military operations against Iran or the Houthis in Yemen, according to the report.
Trump has nevertheless once again instructed military officials to prepare strike options. Last Friday, senior administration officials discussed the plans during a meeting at Camp David led by Vice President JD Vance. The discussions centered on a short but powerful operation lasting approximately three days, targeting Iran's missile and drone capabilities, significant portions of which have been restored by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps since the opening stages of the war. Other potential targets under consideration include energy facilities, Revolutionary Guard headquarters and command centers.
'We are prepared for negotiations and do not fear them'
The future of the confrontation with Iran remains deeply uncertain. Negotiations between Tehran and Washington have produced no breakthrough, clashes over the Strait of Hormuz continue, and an agreement over Iran's nuclear program appears increasingly distant.
Iranian forces continue to issue threats and assert their military capabilities, while U.S. officials maintain that their operations have achieved major results. The approaching elections in both Israel and the United States have also raised questions in Tehran about how domestic political considerations could influence future military decisions.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Thursday that indirect negotiations with Washington were continuing and that Tehran was considering the American response to its proposed diplomatic framework. "The negotiation process is continuing, and messages are being exchanged through mediators," Araghchi said. "We presented our proposal for a seven-day plan and heard the American position regarding it. We are now reviewing that position, and I believe we will provide our response in the coming days."
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei also said in recent days that Tehran had clarified its conditions for ending the war on all fronts and restoring security in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. He confirmed that messages were being exchanged between Iran and the United States through intermediaries. Despite those statements, Trump has already rejected the seven-day proposal Iran presented in September.
According to reports, the plan called for a weeklong suspension of hostile activities throughout the region, including Lebanon, the release of $12 billion in frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports and an end to the American blockade of Iranian ports. It also included guarantees concerning respect for Iranian sovereignty, commitments related to a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington, and an end to threats against Iran.
Under the proposal, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz on the seventh day if its conditions were met. Tehran has continued to insist on those demands despite Washington's rejection. Iranian government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani reiterated the country's position last week. "We are prepared for negotiations and do not fear them," she said. "We will defend our country, whether through war or through negotiations."
Iran also appears to be developing longer-term plans for the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic maritime passage connecting the Persian Gulf to international shipping routes. Tehran has been holding discussions with Oman, which lies on the opposite side of the strait, concerning its future management.
Last week, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman said the two countries had agreed on the locations of safe shipping passages and reached an understanding on how to present the arrangements to the relevant international organization. That process, he said, would move forward soon.
Iranian state-aligned media have continued reporting incidents involving vessels accused of violating Tehran's maritime regulations in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials insist that the waterway remains under the complete control of their forces and that the current restrictions will continue until Tehran's demands are met. Washington disputes those claims. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last week that Iran had "completely lost" control of the strait.
Alongside the dispute over Hormuz, Iran's nuclear program has returned to the center of diplomatic discussions. On Wednesday, a senior source told the Saudi-owned Al Arabiya television network that control of the waterway was no longer Washington's main priority.
"Hormuz is no longer a priority for Washington after Iran lost control of it," the source said. "Progress in negotiations depends on Iran's response to Trump's demands regarding its nuclear capabilities. Washington is demanding that Iran acknowledge that it will not continue developing those capabilities."
On September 28, a senior U.S. official told Al Jazeera that there would be no agreement without addressing Iran's nuclear program. The official said Trump was prepared to ease sanctions on Iran and release frozen Iranian assets in exchange for progress on the nuclear issue.
Tehran, however, has shown little willingness to compromise on what it describes as its right to enrich uranium. Last week, a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran would never surrender that right and that Washington's position on the nuclear program directly contradicted Tehran's demands.
Mohammad Eslami, head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, reiterated that position Thursday. "We will not give up our right to enrichment, nor will we hand over our uranium," he said. "Nuclear negotiations were not on the agenda, and the American statements stem from desperation."
Iran threatens to expand attacks beyond Hormuz
As diplomatic contacts continue, Iranian military officials have maintained an increasingly confrontational tone, warning that further American attacks could trigger a broader escalation. Over the weekend, the Revolutionary Guards warned that their operations against vessels accused of violating Iranian regulations would no longer be confined to the Strait of Hormuz.
"From now on, action against violating vessels will not be limited to the Strait of Hormuz," the Revolutionary Guards said. "Any vessel traveling along an unauthorized route, anywhere in the region, will be punished."
Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi issued a similar warning last week, saying Iranian naval forces were prepared to respond decisively to what Tehran considers hostile actions or unauthorized maritime movements. "The naval forces are prepared to respond decisively to any miscalculation by the enemy and to the passage of vessels without authorization," he said.
Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohabbi has also warned in recent weeks that another attack on Iran would prompt a fundamental change in Tehran's military strategy. "If another attack takes place, our defensive strategy will change, including expanding the geographical scope of the confrontation, using new equipment and weapons, and selecting different targets," he said. "Iran possesses strategic capabilities and targets that have not yet been used, but they will be activated if necessary."
Although such warnings form part of Iran's continuing propaganda campaign, several Western reports published in recent days suggest Tehran retains substantial military capabilities despite the sustained bombing campaign. Last week, satellite imagery reportedly revealed significant renewed activity at Min-Zadai, a nuclear weapons development complex northeast of Tehran that Israel previously exposed and attacked during Operation Roaring Lion.
The reported activity has added to concerns over how much of Iran's military and strategic infrastructure has survived the war and how quickly damaged facilities can be restored.
At the same time, Iran's political leadership has been urging national unity and domestic stability while acknowledging the mounting challenges facing the country. Years of sanctions, the economic consequences of the war and persistent social pressures have left Iran confronting serious internal difficulties. Differences also remain within the Iranian leadership and political establishment over the possibility of reaching an agreement with the United States.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged those challenges last week, calling for practical solutions and closer cooperation across government institutions and society. "In light of the challenges posed by the war and sanctions, solving the country's problems requires practical plans, cooperation and coordination among all government bodies and sectors of society," he said. "We must work to address economic and social problems while preserving national unity and avoiding confrontation."

articles.title: Finland to supply Ukraine with F-16s ammunition ‘in the coming days:' Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that Finland would supply Ukraine with ammunition for F-16 fighter jets “in the coming days,” adding that the weapons would help counter jet-powered Shahed drones.
In a statement on US social media company X, Zelenskyy said he had spoken by phone with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and French President Emmanuel Macron to discuss Russian attacks on Kyiv and further support for Ukraine.
Zelenskyy told Stubb about the latest Russian strikes and warned that additional Russian revenue from petroleum product exports could finance the Russia-Ukraine war, referring to an agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on diesel supplies to the US and global markets.
“Of course, we also discussed a new challenge: additional revenue for Russia from petroleum product exports, which can be used to finance further Russian aggression,” Zelenskyy said.
He added that the two sides were preparing meetings and coordinating steps “that can be useful under the current circumstances.”
Stubb said on X that Finland had announced its 35th support package for Ukraine on Friday, stressing: “We are doing everything we can to protect Ukrainian civilians.”
In his conversation with Macron, Zelenskyy discussed the risks posed by easing restrictions on Russian oil products, saying Moscow “must feel that they no longer have the potential to prolong the war.”
“The need for additional air defense packages for Ukraine is obvious, and we are working with all partners toward the appropriate decisions,” Zelenskyy said, warning that the threat of further Russian missile strikes remained particularly high in the days to come.
Russian attack on Kyiv
Zelenskyy said his call with Macron took place amid a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv and repeated strikes on energy facilities with jet-powered Shahed drones.
“What allowing Russia to sell oil products means was heard most clearly in Kyiv just now, when, after repeated attacks on energy facilities with jet-powered 'Shaheds,' Russia launched a ballistic missile attack as well,” he said, adding that some missiles had been intercepted.
Zelenskyy said every additional billion dollars Russia earned from exports would go toward acquiring critical components and equipment for weapons production, upgrading Shahed drones, manufacturing missiles and recruiting more foreign fighters.
“Russia’s choice is war,” he said, adding that Moscow would agree to end the conflict only when it felt its ability to prolong it was diminishing.
He argued that “signals” Russia received the previous day had instead suggested it could continue attacking Ukraine.
“And this needs to be corrected,” Zelenskyy said, calling on the US, Europe and other partners to send “stronger signals” in support of Ukraine and restrict Russia’s ability to wage war.

articles.title: Russian Ballistic Strike on Kyiv Injures 6 in Restaurant
articles.body:
Russian forces launched a ballistic missile attack against Kyiv on Saturday, Oct. 10, striking a restaurant building in the capital’s northern Obolonskyi district, injuring six people, and scattering missile debris across a nearby residential courtyard, municipal authorities reported.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed the casualties and destruction on his official Telegram channel, stating that firefighters and emergency crews deployed to contain a blaze at the damaged restaurant and administer emergency aid to the victims.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“In the Obolonskyi district, there was a hit on a restaurant building. At another address in Obolon, missile debris fell in the courtyard of a residential building,” Klitschko said.
The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) confirmed that missile fragments landed in an open area adjacent to residential housing in the district, noting that specialized emergency brigades and law enforcement teams were dispatched to verify whether any casualties had occurred.
The ballistic barrage followed repeated waves of turbojet-powered strike drones earlier in the day that damaged regional power distribution nodes, shut down the capital’s metro system, and disrupted municipal water supplies.
Ukrainian air defense units intercepted a portion of the incoming ballistic missiles over the metropolitan area, but falling wreckage and kinetic impacts damaged civilian structures.
Belarus Summons Ukraine Envoy Over Alleged Bryansk Drone Strike
Later, Klitschko reported that the number of victims had risen to 6. Five of the injured were hospitalized. One person was treated at the scene.
Zelensky links ballistic strike to oil sanctions relief
Speaking following the attack, President Volodymyr Zelensky linked the daylight ballistic assault directly to recent Western commercial accommodations permitting Russian petroleum exports.
The president warned that granting Moscow access to international energy markets generates fresh financial resources that are immediately funneled into expanding the Kremlin’s arsenal of ballistic weapons and high-speed loitering munitions.
“What it means to permit Russia to sell petroleum products was heard best in Kyiv today, when after numerous deployments of jet-powered Shaheds against energy facilities, a ballistic attack also began,” Zelensky stated.
“A portion of the missiles was downed. This demonstrates once again what Russia’s true intentions are. They count on continuing the war, terrorizing ordinary people, and destroying infrastructure.”
Zelensky stressed that international sanctions enforcement remains the only viable mechanism to limit the Kremlin’s capacity to sustain long-range bombardments.
“Every additional billion dollars they are able to earn from exports will be spent on precisely this: searching for and importing critical components, equipment for arms manufacturing, reinforcing Shaheds, producing missiles, and recruiting additional mercenaries for the front line,” Zelensky said.
“Yesterday, unfortunately, there were entirely different signals for Russia – signals that continuing attacks is supposedly permissible. This must be corrected. Strong signals are needed from the United States, Europe, and other partners.”
Bilateral consultations with Macron under fire
During the ballistic bombardment, Zelensky held an urgent telephone consultation with French President Emmanuel Macron to coordinate defense assistance and diplomatic responses to sanctions easing.
Zelensky expressed gratitude to Paris for continuous solidarity, emphasizing that the intensifying combination of ballistic missiles and turbine-powered drones necessitates expedited deliveries of modern air defense complexes and interceptors.
“It was precisely during today’s Russian ballistic attack against Kyiv that we spoke with the President of France,” Zelensky said.
“The need for additional air defense packages for Ukraine is obvious, and we are working with all partners for corresponding decisions. Unfortunately, a distinct threat of further missile strikes persists these days. It is vital to increase pressure on Russia in response, and joint bold steps must follow.”
Zelensky reported that discussions with Macron focused heavily on joint countermeasures to reverse the dilution of energy sanctions against Moscow.
“We discussed the challenges stemming from the easing of sanctions against petroleum products,” Zelensky added.
“The Russians must feel that their potential to prolong the war will no longer exist. We are coordinating substantively and preparing upcoming meetings.”
Compounding infrastructure crisis in the capital
The ballistic strikes capped a day of intense aerial bombardment that strained municipal services and civilian infrastructure across Kyiv.
Earlier on Saturday morning, Russian drone strikes damaged a major energy installation in Kyiv region, precipitating voltage drops that paralyzed all three lines of the Kyiv metro network, halted municipal electric surface transport across multiple districts, and forced energy operators to introduce emergency blackouts in Pivdenna Borshchahivka.
The grid instability also knocked offline regional water pumping stations, leaving taps dry across large parts of the capital.
Concurrently, falling drone debris struck an eight-story commercial office building and a 25-story residential tower in the Solomianskyi district, alongside fragments landing in Podilskyi district.

articles.title: Iran retains missile, drone production capabilities despite months of US-Israeli strikes - report
articles.body:
Iran has retained the ability to manufacture ballistic missiles and drones despite eight months of US and Israeli airstrikes, allowing Tehran to replenish its weapons stockpiles as US President Donald Trump debates delaying further military action until after the November midterm elections, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing Western officials familiar with intelligence assessments.
The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Iran had preserved parts of its weapons manufacturing infrastructure despite extensive strikes targeting its military-industrial capabilities.
One Western official assessed that Tehran still possesses significant stocks of ballistic missiles and certain anti-ship weapons, with the capacity to manufacture additional munitions relatively quickly.
The official also claimed that Russia has been supplying Iran with missiles, consistent with a separate intelligence assessment from June. Russia's Defense Ministry did not respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.
The findings contrast with repeated assertions by Trump administration officials that the US-Israeli military campaign has effectively dismantled Iran's ability to threaten American military installations and regional allies.
Trump previously described Iran's military as "totally destroyed," while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on September 30 that US operations had destroyed Iran's "military industrial capacity" and "their entire defense base."
White House disputes assessment of Iran's military capabilities
White House spokesperson Anna Kelly rejected the Western officials' assessment, defending the effectiveness of American operations against Iran's nuclear and conventional military infrastructure.
“First, President Trump obliterated Iran’s nuclear facilities during Operation Midnight Hammer,” Kelly said in a statement.
“Then, Operation Epic Fury successfully destroyed the conventional shield that Iran sought to create over a nuclear program, including their ballistic missiles, production facilities, and navy.”
The extent of damage to Iran's missile industry has remained disputed. A September report, citing US and Middle Eastern officials, indicated that Tehran had resumed limited ballistic missile production using existing components, including at underground facilities, although manufacturing remained below prewar levels.
Trump announced on Thursday that the US would refrain from attacking Iran before the November midterm elections, after previously considering renewed military strikes amid escalating attacks on commercial shipping.
The pause could provide Tehran with additional time to restore production and replenish its arsenals, according to the Western assessments.
Iran has intensified attacks on vessels operating near the Strait of Hormuz, with at least 10 ships struck over the preceding week, according to the UK Navy.
The attacks have increased concerns about maritime security and potential disruption to global energy supplies, particularly as the US continues its naval blockade of Iranian oil exports.
In September, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that it could deploy different weapons and strike new targets if Washington launched another offensive, signaling its intention to maintain military pressure despite the damage sustained during the war.
Iran's remaining missile arsenal raises questions
The US-Israeli air campaign likely inflicted significant long-term damage on Iran's prewar missile production infrastructure, according to an assessment by Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst and visiting research fellow at King's College London.
However, the precise size of Iran's remaining arsenal remains uncertain.
Israeli estimates placed Tehran's ballistic missile stockpile at approximately 2,500 before the war, while Western intelligence assessments in June suggested Iran still possessed roughly three-quarters of its prewar munitions.
Earlier Israeli military assessments indicated that extensive strikes on Iranian military-industrial facilities could require years of reconstruction, although the ability to restore launchers and other components remained a concern.
The discrepancy between assessments of Iran's remaining stockpiles and its manufacturing capacity highlights the difficulty of determining how much military capability Tehran can regenerate without further external assistance.
A separate August assessment described how Iran had used periods of reduced fighting to repair launchers, restore access to underground facilities and accelerate efforts to rebuild missile and drone production. Analysts cautioned that such activity did not necessarily mean Tehran had recovered its full prewar capabilities.
For Washington and Israel, Iran's continued access to ballistic missiles and anti-ship weapons raises concerns about its ability to retaliate against renewed military action.
With the Islamic Republic facing mounting economic pressure from the US naval blockade, Western officials assessed that Tehran could increasingly rely on asymmetric operations, including attacks on maritime traffic, to impose costs on its militarily superior adversaries.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine needs a new president who will agree to end the war
articles.body:
Trump says Ukraine needs a new president who will agree to end the war
US leader suggests Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war amid tensions with Kyiv over a diesel deal with Russia.
United States President Donald Trump says Ukraine should replace Volodymyr Zelenskyy with a new leader, lashing out at him for Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries that have contributed to high diesel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” Trump said at the White House on Saturday, adding that “for some reason [Zelenskyy] never does.”
Trump said that under Zelenskyy, Ukraine has “lost 30 percent of your country and you’ve had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That’s a war that should have never have started. And I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Following the remarks, Ukraine’s foreign minister defended Zelenskyy. “He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide,” Andriy Sybiga said in a post on X. “Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support.”
Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to reduce high fuel prices ahead of the US midterms, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure.
He has also sought to blame record-high US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.
Trump suggested on Saturday that if he had been US president in 2022 “that war would have never started”.
“There was no reason that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence,” he said.
The remarks came hours after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, according to Ukrainian officials.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than four and a half years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed at least 60 people over the past four days.
Anger in Kyiv over diesel deal
On Friday, Trump said he had struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of Washington’s pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine.
He said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional three million tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he added.
The move drew a furious reaction from Zelenskyy. After Russia’s strikes on Saturday, he wrote on X: “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia”.
Zelenskyy said the attacks show Moscow understands “any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities.”
The president said every additional billion dollars Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries, and that Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defences, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days.
He also said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and that Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16s used to intercept Shahed drones.
Ukraine’s European allies have expressed dismay at the Russian deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions.
Trump’s announcement about the deal was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel the war against Ukraine.
Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami on Friday to discuss a proposal to end the war.

articles.title: US military has lost 81 aircraft in Iran war according to Congressional report
articles.body:
Eighty-one aircraft in the US military have been destroyed or damaged during the war with Iran, a congressional Research Service report released this week said.
Among the aircraft lost are some of the most advanced weapons in the US arsenal, including the F-35A fighter jet and the E-3 Sentry, which has four jet engines and a radar dome on its fuselage used to track targets and manage airspace during engagements.
MQ-9 Reaper drones accounted for more than half of the losses found in the report. Reaper drones are used in the Iran war for gathering intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.
The total cost of the aircraft lost since February is between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion, according to the report, which cited figures from the congressional Budget Office.
US Central Command estimated that the ongoing war with Iran has cost the US roughly $44 billion total in September. However, that number does not include damage to infrastructure at US bases in the Middle East, according to reporting from the Washington Post.
CNN reported that some of the aircraft may have returned to service after being damaged, including eight F-15 Strike Eagle fighter jets after they were damaged during an Iranian strike on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on the night of September 8.
The report examined statements and figures from the Department of Defense; its inspector general; CENTCOM; and external media reports reviewed by the CRS.
Senators accuse Pentagon of withholding information
Bipartisan criticism of the Pentagon has mounted over defense officials' unwillingness to be transparent with Congress about the cost of the Iran war and the Trump administration’s National Defense Strategy.
Following a meeting with Defense Undersecretary Elbridge Colby and the Senate Armed Services Committee, Senator Jacky Rose of Nevada said Colby “was not forthcoming” and “did not really address our concerns or issues.”
In a separate instance this week, US Senator Chris Murphy said on Tuesday that the US Defense Department denied him access to a key military base in Qatar during a visit to the Middle East. He described it as part of a US government effort to conceal the impact of the Iran war.
"This trip confirmed for me that there is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and the American people," Murphy told a group of journalists in Riyadh, the second stop on his trip.
Analysts cited by CNN said actions in the Middle East, including the Iran war and conflicts with Iran’s proxies, have taken a toll on the MQ-9 Reaper drones. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told Congress that the MQ-9 was the “most valuable player” in the war with Iran
The US military is believed to have roughly 135 MQ-9 drones in its arsenal, the Air Force Times reported in May, 2026.
The military lost 45 of the drones in the Middle East this year alone, in what the Atlantic Council describes as losses at an “alarming rate.”
The US military has not experienced loss of aircraft at such a rate since Operation Desert Storm in 1991.

articles.title: Putin’s Vile Chess
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has “played” the Game of Kings, or chess, against Ukraine and the West for years, but badly. But his attempt to conquer Ukraine has been disastrous.
Putin misread the board, opened in 2022 with a “blitzkrieg gambit,” expecting Kyiv to fall quickly, then overextended his “pieces” and lost the initiative.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He underestimated his opponent – notably Ukrainian courage, resilience, and technological innovation – and miscalculated Western cohesion. He then shifted into a horrific war of attrition, sacrificing 1.5 million men, spending $770 million a day, and squandering $680 billion since 2022, in return for minuscule territorial gains.
Now, Putin has decided to conduct saturation bombing attacks on Ukrainian women and children in Kyiv and other cities to bring the country to its knees. This is another blunder, like a “poisoned-pawn” mistake in chess, when a player gobbles up easily captured pieces but totally undermines his position and costs himself the game.
Russia’s war against Ukraine is fought on two chessboards. One involves missiles, drones, soldiers, and oil refineries. The other is a diplomatic chessboard involving Putin, US President Donald Trump, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, and Europe.
Putin has started to pound Ukrainian civilians, power, transport, and water facilities before winter to create a humanitarian disaster that will spill over into Europe. But his brutality backfires and upsets Americans and Europeans. It also exposes the stupidity of pursuing peace deals with Putin or falling for anything he says, including his thinly disguised “bribery” attempt to sell a Russian oil company to a group of Trump’s friends. It’s blood money. It’s also insulting.
Russian Ballistic Strike on Kyiv Injures 6 in Restaurant
In return for killing innocents intentionally, Russia should be booted from the UN and Trump must disinvite Putin from attending the G20 conference in December, then unleash the sledgehammer sanctions just given to him by Congress.
Fortunately, Kyiv and Ukrainians are tough. Blowing up and burning data centers provide striking visuals on Russian television, but Kyiv’s internet system, battle-tested for ages, is too decentralized to be shut down easily.
The same is true when it comes to keeping the power on. Ukrainians have learned to be good at repairing and replacing everything since the war started in 2022, and they are also psychologically resolute. Life in the capital continues. Concerts, fashion shows, baby showers happen as drones attack constantly. Schools operate in subways. Parliament now meets underground because of bombing attacks.
Says a close friend of mine in Kyiv: “There are long lineups at banks, grocery stores, and everything takes ten times longer to do. My friend’s due date is in two weeks, and she’s busy planning for her new baby, but buying formula and diapers is more difficult. But she’ll find a way. If the only choice is to give up to Russia, I don’t choose it, nor does anyone else. We stock up on what we need and use the shelters. It will get worse, and everyone’s preparing. We understand. It will be fine. I will be fine.”
In recent days, Zelensky issued an “SOS” to Ukrainians, confirming that Putin will ruthlessly escalate this autumn: “We know from intelligence and some people around Putin that at the beginning of September Putin said, ‘No rules now.’ The Russians couldn’t occupy us. So now they are doing massive attacks and massive killings. And of course, they want to go after our bridges and, from what we understand, after our data centers, internet, cell network, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to run away from their cities, and we need to do everything to save our people and cities.”
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s deep strikes have wrecked 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity, dramatically reducing the cash flow it needs to wage war. And the more war crimes Putin commits, the more pushbacks.
After Putin’s latest threat against civilians, Germany immediately announced another €1 billion ($1.12 billion) in military assistance, including long-range weapons, drones and satellite capabilities, and that German and Ukrainian companies are deepening defense-industrial cooperation.
Then on Oct. 4, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz even flew into Kyiv during a bombing attack to show support for Ukraine. “I traveled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks. If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us. And I will tell President Zelensky today: ‘You can continue to count on our help,’” Merz said.
Meanwhile, midterms approach in the US on Nov. 5, and Trump’s questionable, tepid, and foolish respect for Putin will do him in because the American public is simply not buying it, any more than they agree that his Iran war is a good idea. His popularity is at an all-time low due to corrupt practices, economic pain, and the Iran war. Russia is considered a scourge, not a potential G20 ally.
A major survey this week by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found that 86% of Americans blame Putin for the conflict. A YouGov poll found that 61% of Americans believe Russia started the war and only 6% blame Ukraine. Some 74% of Americans believe Putin’s invasion was unjustified and support weapons for Ukraine and lethal economic sanctions against Russia. And last month, Congress overwhelmingly approved a sledgehammer sanctions bill that Trump signed. In response, Putin snubbed this “leverage” by launching a bombing holocaust against civilians. Trump cannot ignore this.
Putin’s declaration that he will be murdering women and children, and destroying cities, is his “poison pawn” that undermines any credibility he may have had. Peace talks are pointless; only more weapons and sanctions are needed.
Obviously, Putin has never wanted peace and has been stringing Trump along. His threat to women and children in Ukraine is sufficient justification for Trump to use his sledgehammer sanctions, which are capable of strangling Russia’s cash flow and stopping his war. Trump must also remove all restrictions on Ukraine’s use of ATACMS, provide Patriots, and help fund Ukrainian defense production. Then Europe must release to Ukraine the $200 billion in frozen Russian central bank assets it holds in order to help it pay for weapons, defense, and repairs.
Putin must be defeated. Checkmate. He is not civilized, nor is his regime. He never wanted peace; he will never leave Ukraine alone; he wants Europe; he spreads war globally, and when it’s over, the West must provide Ukraine with arms and credible security guarantees backed by troops.
Putin hides with his family and cohorts in bunkers, as did Hitler in the end, and issues a declaration to slaughter innocents, which has gone too far. He has defeated himself and ended up in “zugzwang”, a situation in chess where every move worsens his military or economic position, including doing nothing.
Putin must go. He belongs in a gulag or on trial at The Hague or worse. This must end.

articles.title: Exclusive: 'It felt like a trap,' how Ukraine was blindsided by Trump's Putin pivot
articles.body:
Exclusive: 'It felt like a trap.' How Ukraine was blindsided by Trump's Putin pivot
U.S. President Donald Trump and Russia's President Vladimir Putin arrive for a press conference at Joint Base Elmendorf- Richardson, Aug. 15, 2025, in Anchorage, Alaska. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)
When U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner told Ukraine's delegation on Oct. 9 that President Donald Trump was preparing to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, the Ukrainians struggled to believe what they were hearing.
The delegation had traveled to the United States to discuss a possible energy ceasefire with Russia. Instead, Kyiv's negotiators found themselves blindsided by a decision they feared would hand Moscow fresh revenue to finance its war against Ukraine while undermining Kyiv's leverage in negotiations.
"It was not just our delegation there, but a European one as well," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent. "It's just that everyone was sitting there like fools."
Washington was asking Ukraine to restrain its attacks on Russian energy while giving Moscow an economic reprieve — all as Trump faced consequences from the war against Iran.
"And yet he's the one who got everyone dragged into a war in Iran — a war with no way out — and is selling us out… Just to get a temporary, deceptive reprieve a few weeks before the election," the official said.
The Kyiv Independent spoke with several Ukrainian officials involved in or close to the negotiations. All of them were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
For Ukraine, the key question was why Kyiv should surrender a major means of pressuring Moscow if Russia faced no obligation to stop attacking Ukraine's energy system.
A deal Kyiv never saw coming
President Volodymyr Zelensky had sent a Ukrainian delegation to the United States for talks scheduled for Oct. 9-10. The agenda included a possible energy ceasefire with Moscow and a separate arrangement to halt attacks in the Black Sea.
Instead, the talks were derailed after Trump announced that Russia would supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Kyiv had not been informed of the decision in advance. Although Zelensky publicly acknowledged that Washington was considering a deal with Moscow, Ukrainian officials said they had not known the details before the announcement that evening.
For the delegation, the revelation raised questions about whether Washington had already negotiated terms with Moscow while Ukrainian and European officials were still trying to establish the parameters of an energy truce.
"It felt like a trap," the senior Ukrainian official said.
"To be honest, everyone was shocked as f*ck."
The timing of the U.S. decision only deepened the suspicion.
Following Trump's direction, the U.S. Treasury Department announced that its Office of Foreign Assets Control was "immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
One Ukrainian official pointed to April 7, the date on which the waiver was set to expire, as evidence that Washington had planned the measure around a specific timetable.
"They lifted the sanctions until April 7... So they were preparing this for Oct. 7. It's a birthday present for Putin. They're counting the six months," the official said.
Trump's demand to stop Ukraine's strikes
The dispute had been building for weeks.
Trump had previously pressed Zelensky to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities, arguing that Kyiv should stop disrupting Russia's fuel production.
"Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump told Zelensky on Sept. 13.
Kyiv rejected the premise that Ukraine should halt its strikes unilaterally. Ukrainian officials said Zelensky had repeatedly made clear that any energy ceasefire would have to apply to both sides, with Russia also stopping its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
That distinction is central to Kyiv. Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, terminals, and other energy facilities aim to disrupt a major source of funding for Moscow's war effort. Russia, meanwhile, has systematically targeted Ukrainian power plants and substations, seeking to deprive civilians of electricity and heating.
A ceasefire that stopped only Ukrainian attacks would therefore leave Russia's campaign against Ukraine's energy system intact while protecting infrastructure that helps sustain the Russian war machine.
Yet, Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that U.S. negotiators presented the issue differently during the talks, framing Zelensky as responsible for the impasse because he had refused to halt attacks on Russian refineries.
The Ukrainians were also told that Washington would cut off intelligence sharing that has helped Kyiv identify and strike targets inside Russia, one person present at the talks told the Kyiv Independent.
U.S. intelligence has played an important role in Ukrainian attacks, and restricting access to it would weaken Kyiv's ability to conduct strikes deep inside Russian territory.
One senior Ukrainian official involved in the talks responded with bitter humor.
"I hope the Americans don't give them Patriot (air defense systems) to protect their oil refineries," the official said.
The remark, however, captured a broader fear in Kyiv.
Washington already ended up helping Moscow shield the infrastructure that finances its war while pressuring Ukraine to surrender a means of striking back.
Another senior Ukrainian official said Ukraine had not agreed to stop attacking Russian refineries and would not commit to doing so without reciprocal Russian action.
For Kyiv, the principle remained unchanged. An energy truce could work only if both countries accepted the same restrictions.
"It was just f**king stupid to bury the idea of an energy truce with that move," one official said, suggesting that Washington was trying to strip Ukraine of its greatest source of leverage in the negotiations.
The war continues on both sides
Events on the ground showed how little the announcement had changed.
Just hours after Trump's announcement, Ukrainian drones struck an oil loading terminal in Russia's Rostov-on-Don. The terminal handles petroleum products for export and supplies fuel to Russia's military.
Russia, meanwhile, launched a drone attack followed by a missile strike on Kyiv on Oct. 10, also targeting Ukrainian energy facilities.
Neither side had agreed to stop striking energy infrastructure, and the U.S. announcement had done little to bridge the gap between their positions.
Zelensky addressed the decision in a voice message to reporters late on Oct. 9, warning that allowing Russia to export diesel would just give Moscow additional revenue to sustain its war.
"This only fuels Putin and enables him to wage more war," Zelensky said. "And at the moment when we are talking about peace, the U.S. is allowing Russia to export diesel."
He also questioned the purpose of sending a Ukrainian delegation to negotiations under those circumstances.
"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. This is certainly not honest, and it is certainly not how partners should act," Zelensky said, calling the decision "a weak decision by our strong partners."
Ukraine was being asked to make concessions on the battlefield even as Moscow continued to attack its cities and energy infrastructure.
For one senior Ukrainian official, the explanation for Washington's move was straightforward: Trump was trying to deflect blame for the consequences of his own foreign policy.
"Clearly, Trump doesn't want to admit that it was his war against Iran that caused so many problems for Americans," the official said.

articles.title: Drones Strike Rostov Oil Terminal, Igniting Major Fire
articles.body:
Ukrainian strike drones attacked an oil transshipment terminal in the southern Russian port city of Rostov-on-Don early Saturday morning, Oct. 10, igniting a large blaze at the facility, Russian regional officials and independent media reported.
Residents across Rostov-on-Don reported multiple explosions and visible air defense fire beginning late Friday evening and continuing into the early morning hours.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Rostov Regional Governor Yuriy Slyusar confirmed an aerial attack and a subsequent fire in the regional center, stating that emergency responders deployed to contain the blaze and claiming no casualties were recorded.
Slyusar said Russian air defense forces intercepted at least 50 unmanned aerial vehicles across the Rostov region between Friday evening and Saturday morning.
Open-source intelligence analysts from independent Russian news outlet Astra geolocated footage published by local residents, verifying that the fire broke out at the “Yug Rusi” oil products transshipment terminal in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny district.
The facility functions as a key logistics node for petroleum products, handling transshipment from the Novoshakhtinsk Petroleum Products Plant (NZNP) and other regional suppliers.
Operating with a designed annual handling capacity of approximately 2.5 million metric tons, the terminal processes fuel supplies utilized by the Russian armed forces and facilitates maritime export shipments generating foreign currency revenue.
Putin Touts 90% Dollar-Free CIS Trade as Russia Sidesteps Western Sanctions
Although commercially known as Yug Rusi since its commissioning alongside the first phase of the Novoshakhtinsk refinery in 2009, corporate filings by the Novoshakhtinsk plant designate the facility as the “NZNP oil loading terminal, Rostov branch.” The terminal was previously targeted by Ukrainian drone strikes in July.
Strategic targeting of Russian fuel and refining logistics
The strike in Rostov-on-Don forms part of a systematic Ukrainian asymmetric campaign targeting fuel depots, refineries, and chemical production hubs that sustain Moscow’s military operations.
The overnight attack follows coordinated long-range strikes on Oct. 9 that damaged Russian energy and industrial assets across western and central regions.
Drones struck the Redkino Experimental Plant in the Tver region, igniting a fire at the chemical facility, which manufactures Decylin-M – a specialized liquid fuel component utilized in Russian Kh-55 and Kh-101 strategic cruise missiles – alongside fuel additives for aviation kerosene and diesel.
Concurrently on Oct. 9, Ukrainian strikes hit an oil depot north of Belgorod that supplies fuel to industrial enterprises and transport fleets across the border region, while a separate drone strike damaged a major Yandex data center in Kaluga, disabling multiple server modules for the second consecutive day following an earlier strike on a company facility in Sasovo, Ryazan region.
Extended-range interdiction
Ukrainian precision units have progressively expanded their operational strike radius against Russian petrochemical infrastructure deep inside Russia.
On Thursday, Oct. 8, Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces (SSO) announced they conducted a second deep-interdiction strike against the Omsk Oil Refinery in southwestern Siberia, situated roughly 2,500 kilometers (1,550 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Operating alongside the domestic Russian insurgent movement “Chernaya Iskra” (Black Spark), SSO long-range strike drones navigated flight routes approaching 3,000 kilometers to strike distillation units at the Siberian plant.
Ukrainian defense and security officials have emphasized that degrading refining capacity, export terminals, and frontline fuel stockpiles directly constrains the mobility of Russian mechanized units while diminishing state export earnings that fund the Kremlin’s wartime budget.

articles.title: Ukraine attacks Russia with spy balloons
articles.body:
Ukraine attacks Russia with spy balloons
Ukrainian spy balloons have been spotted over central Russia’s Yaroslavl Region for the first time, according to the regional Security Ministry.
Local authorities said several of the small flying objects were successfully shot down on Friday, urging residents to report anything suspicious that they see in the sky or suspected debris to emergency services.
The balloons “had been launched from the territory of Ukraine,” according to officials. Small reconnaissance balloons can be used to distract enemy air defenses, but they can also serve as reconnaissance platforms, including to pinpoint the locations of air defense systems or help direct strikes against other targets.
Yaroslavl Region has been targeted by Ukrainian long-range strikes in recent weeks. In mid-September, the Russian military shot down 65 drones over the region in a single day during a large-scale drone raid targeting a local refinery.
Although Friday’s incident was the first of its kind reported in Yaroslavl Region, the Russian military has encountered Ukrainian spy balloons and even explosive-laden balloons in the past.
In September 2025, the Ukrainian military attempted to strike several Russian regions with dozens of meteorological balloons carrying explosives.
The Wall Street Journal claimed in a February article that Kiev had been using high-altitude balloons in attacks on Russia since the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022. However, according to the Russian Defense Ministry, such attacks were first detected in autumn 2024, with another surge in reported incidents in late summer 2025.
The recent balloon attacks come as Russia has stepped up strikes on missile and drone warehouses, as well as unmanned aerial vehicle assembly facilities, in response to continued Ukrainian strikes on Russian civilian and energy infrastructure, which Moscow describes as terrorist acts.
After Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky recently threatened to step up attacks on Russian oil refineries, Moscow vowed to intensify strikes on Ukraine’s military-related facilities while maintaining that it never targets civilians.
On Wednesday, the Russian military targeted a Smart Ammunition facility used to assemble and store FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, FP-9 tactical ballistic missiles, and components for both weapons, as well as other sites across several Ukrainian regions, including a drone workshop in Kirovograd Region and the JTI Ukraine tobacco factory in Kremenchug, which Russian officials say is used to manufacture small-arms ammunition.

articles.title: Finland to send F-16 ammunition to Ukraine within days
articles.body:
Finland will supply ammunition for Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets within the coming days, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Saturday, 10 October, following a telephone conversation with Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
The delivery forms part of Finland's 35th military assistance package to Ukraine, valued at approximately €1 million, as Russia intensifies missile and drone attacks across the country.
Zelenskyy disclosed the planned shipment in a Facebook post following his discussion with Stubb. He said the ammunition would help Ukrainian forces intercept Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, which Moscow has deployed in attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
The Ukrainian president did not specify the type or quantity of ammunition Finland would provide.
Stubb also confirmed the conversation in a post on X, stating that air defence was a central component of Finland's latest military assistance package.
The Finnish Ministry of Defence announced the package on Friday, 9 October, after the government accelerated its response to an urgent request from Kyiv.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said Helsinki had brought forward its decision because of Ukraine's immediate defence requirements.
"We will not close our eyes to Ukrainians’ hour of need. Instead, we will stand with Ukraine and continue our materiel assistance deliveries," Häkkänen said in the ministry's statement.
The Finnish president formally approved the shipment on 9 October following a government proposal.
According to the Defence Ministry, the package consists of a single category of military equipment drawn from Finnish Defence Forces stocks.
The announcement brings the total value of Finland's military equipment assistance to Ukraine to approximately €3.6 billion since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Helsinki has also begun preparing another, more extensive assistance package, although officials have not announced its value or expected delivery date.
Ukraine has relied on Western-supplied F-16 aircraft to strengthen its air defences and counter Russian aerial attacks.
Denmark and the Netherlands supplied approximately 40 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine during 2024 and 2025. Ukrainian authorities have not disclosed how many remain operational.
During Saturday's conversation, Zelenskyy and Stubb also discussed the recent agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin concerning Russian diesel supplies to American and international markets.
Russian strikes across south-eastern Ukraine early on Saturday killed 15 people, including three children. Zelenskyy accused Moscow of responding to the US decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports by launching five glide bombs at residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia.
Zelenskyy described the agreement as a new challenge and said Ukraine and Finland were coordinating further diplomatic discussions and responses.
Earlier in the week, Russian attacks reportedly killed nearly 80 civilians across Ukraine over two days.

articles.title: Finland to Supply F-16 Ammunition to Counter Jet Drones, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Ukraine will receive specialized ammunition for its F-16 fighter jets from Finland in the coming days to intercept Russian turbojet-powered strike drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Oct. 10.
Speaking following a telephone consultation with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Zelensky expressed gratitude for Helsinki’s swift defense assistance, emphasizing that the incoming munitions are essential for neutralizing high-speed loitering munitions that challenge ground-based defenses.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I spoke with President of Finland Alexander Stubb. I am particularly grateful for the support package for our sky defense,” Zelensky stated on social media. “In the coming days, we will receive ammunition for F-16s. This is what currently ensures the downing of jet-powered Shaheds.”
The president reported that the bilateral discussion covered recent Russian aerial strikes against Ukrainian cities and municipal infrastructure, as well as joint diplomatic countermeasures to restrict Russian revenues derived from petroleum product exports.
“Naturally, we also discussed a new challenge: additional Russian revenues from the export of petroleum products, which could go toward financing further Russian aggression,” Zelensky said. “We are preparing meetings and coordinating steps that could be useful in the current circumstances.”
Belarus Summons Ukraine Envoy Over Alleged Bryansk Drone Strike
The munitions transfer follows Helsinki’s approval on Friday of its 35th defense materiel assistance package for Kyiv. Valued at approximately €1 million ($1.13 million), the emergency package was expedited following an urgent appeal by Ukrainian defense authorities and drew a single, undisclosed defense asset directly from Finnish military stockpiles.
Rising threat of high-speed turbojet loitering munitions
The provision of aircraft munitions arrives as Ukrainian military commanders warn that Moscow is rapidly transitioning its long-range drone arsenal toward turbine-propelled models that outpace conventional low-altitude interception networks.
Russian forces have accelerated the deployment of jet-powered Shahed variants since July, presenting significant tactical hurdles for mobile air defense fire teams reliant on heavy machine guns and propeller-driven counter-drone aircraft. While baseline piston-engine Shahed-136 drones cruise at speeds between 180 and 200 km/h, current Russian turbojet drones fly at roughly 600 km/h (370 mph).
Ukrainian Air Force commanders anticipate that adversary technology will continue to advance. During an address to a parliamentary investigative commission, Deputy Air Force Commander Colonel Yurii Cherevashenko warned that Russian designers could eventually increase the dash velocity of jet-powered strike drones to between 800 and 900 km/h (500 to 560 mph).
“We have not seen such speeds yet, but we forecast them,” Cherevashenko said.
Cherevashenko noted that jet-powered drones currently constitute roughly 40 percent of unmanned strike waves deployed against Ukraine, with their share reaching up to 60 percent along specific operational axes.
Military planners project that high-speed turbine models could eventually comprise up to 80 percent of all Russian strike drone salvos, drastically compressing warning times and forcing Ukrainian defenders to rely more heavily on combat aviation.
